definition: In computer vision, the Lucas–Kanade method is a widely used differential method for optical flow estimation developed by Bruce D.
details: Lucas and Takeo Kanade. It assumes that the flow is essentially constant in a local neighbourhood of the pixel under consideration, and solves the basic optical flow equations for all the pixels in that neighbourhood, by the least squares criterion. By combining information from several nearby pixels, the Lucas–Kanade method can often resolve the inherent ambiguity of the optical flow equation. It is also less sensitive to image noise than point-wise methods. On the other hand, since it is a purely local method, it cannot provide flow information in the interior of uniform regions of the image.

explainer.lead: The Lucas–Kanade method is a widely used differential method for optical flow estimation. It matters because combining nearby pixels resolves the ambiguity of the basic optical flow equation and reduces noise sensitivity.

tiers.eli5: To tell how things are moving, it looks at a small patch of pixels together instead of one pixel at a time, which gives a steadier answer.
tiers.practitioner: Used to estimate motion between frames by assuming flow is constant in a local neighbourhood and solving by least squares. A pitfall is that this local-constancy assumption breaks down at motion boundaries and large displacements.
tiers.paperLevel: Assumes flow is essentially constant in a local neighbourhood and solves the optical flow equations over that neighbourhood by least squares; it is primarily suited to small motions.

explainer.example: Tracking small shifts between consecutive frames, it fits one flow vector to a small pixel window using least squares.
